INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici curiae are former Republican Members of
the United States House of Representatives who voted
for passage of the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban (as
defined below) and have long-standing experience
addressing matters of public safety, law enforcement,
and firearms policy. Amici share a strong interest in
preserving the constitutional right protected by the
Second Amendment while ensuring that elected
legislatures retain authority to enact lawful measures
protecting public safety.
Representative Peter King represented New York
in the United States House of Representatives for 28
years from 1993 to 2021. He twice served as Chairman
of the House Committee on Homeland Security (2005–
2007 and 2011–2013), in which capacity he worked
closely with federal, state, and local law-enforcement
agencies on counterterrorism and domestic security
issues. Since leaving Congress, Representative King
has continued to work as a consultant on lawenforcement and counterterrorism matters.
Representative King also has a long-standing interest
in federal gun-safety legislation, having introduced or
sponsored major proposals including the bipartisan
Public Safety and Second Amendment Rights
Protection Act, which would have expanded
background checks for commercial firearm sales, and

2


the Denying Firearms and Explosives to Dangerous
Terrorists Act of 2013, which would have authorized
the Attorney General to prevent individuals suspected
of terrorism from purchasin g firearms or explosives.
His experience addressing threats to public safety and
supporting legislation intended to reduce the risks

Representative Christopher Shays represented
Connecticut’s Fourth Congressional District in the
United States House of Re presentatives for 22 years,
from 1987 to 2009. Representative Shays served on
the House Committee on Homeland Security and
chaired the Subcommittee on National Security,
Emerging Threats, and International Relations. In
that capacity, Representative Shays conducted
hearings related to terrorism, first-responder
preparedness, weapons of mass destruction, and
domestic public safety. Representative Shays
cosponsored the 1993 House legislation establishing
federal background-check requirements for firearm
purchases from licensed dealers and later cosponsored
legislation to renew the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban
before its 2004 expiration.
Amici, as former members of Congress, have a
strong interest in promoting public safety by
preventing violence caused by assault weapons,
consistent with the Second Amendment. As members
of Congress who supported the 1994 Assault Weapons
Ban, Amici are well qualified to address the scope of
the assault weapons regulations at issue in the cases
presented here. Amici swore an oath to protect the

3


Constitution and have a profound and abiding
interest in preserving the right of Congress and State
Legislatures to legislate without forfeiting their
powers to do so in the future based on shifting trends.
Amici firmly believe that assault weapons bans are
both necessary to promote public and lawenforcement safety and entirely consistent with the
Second Amendment.

4


SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
In 1994, a bipartisan Congress enacted the Public
Safety and Recreational Firearms Use Protection Act
(the “1994 Assault Weapons Ban”), which prohibited
the manufacture, transfer, and possession of specified
semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity
magazines, subject to the statute’s grandfathering
provisions. Pub. L. No. 103-322, tit. XI, subtit. A, 108
Stat. 1796, 1996 (1994) (formerly codified at 18 U.S.C.
§ 922(v)–(w)). Responding to a series of high-profile
mass shootings in the preceding years, Congress acted
to prevent the further proliferation of highly
dangerous weapons that posed a grave threat to
public and law-enforcement safety. See H.R. Rep. No.
103-489, at 13–15 (1994); see also Jeffrey A. Roth &
Christopher S. Koper, Impacts of the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban: 1994–96, Nat’l Inst. Just. (1999).
I. The 1994 Assault Weapons Ban was passed with
bipartisan support, including dozens of Republicans
who firmly believed that the prohibition of the
specified weapons was a reasonable public-safety
measure and was consistent with their strong respect
for the rights protected by the Second Amendment.
Former Republican Presidents and Republican
Representatives and Senators alike emphatically
endorsed the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban. Former
President Reagan joined fo rmer Presidents Carter
and Ford in a 1994 letter urging Congress to pass the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban, calling it “absolutely
necessary.” Republican members of Congress avowed
their abiding support for the Second Amendment
while also affirming their belief that the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban was an essential measure to fight crime

5


and to protect both the public and law-enforcement
officers from these unusually lethal weapons. While
the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban preceded the Court’s
more recent clarifications of the scope of the Second
Amendment, it was, and remains, consistent with the
Second Amendment’s guarantee of the individual’s
right to possess firearms for self-defense—a right that
is not, and has never been, an absolute freedom to
possess every highly dangerous firearm that new
weapons technologies may devise and make available.
See District of Columbia v. Heller,  554 U.S. 570, 626
(2008).
II. The 1994 Assault Weapons Ban was predicated
on a congressional finding that assault weapons,
including AR-15-style rifles, were unusually
dangerous and were not necessary to preserve
individual citizens’ fundamental Second Amendment
rights. This finding was supported by years of
hearings and empirical evidence demonstrating that
these weapons were “a growing menace to our society”
out of proportion to their numbers. H.R. Rep. No. 103-
489, at 13.
Although assault weapons made up only about one
percent of firearms in circu lation, they rose from 5.9
percent of ATF crime-gun traces in 1990 to 8.1 percent
in 1993. Id. (citing Public Safety and Recreational
Firearms Use Protection Act:  Hearing on H.R. 4296
and H.R. 3527 Before the Subcomm. on Crime & Crim.
J. of the H. Comm. on the Judiciary, 103d Cong. (1994)
(statement of John Magaw, Director, Bureau of
Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms)). They were “18 times
more likely than other guns to be cop-killers, and 16
times more likely to be traced to crime than other

6


firearms.” 140 Cong. Rec. 9338 (May 5, 1994)
(statement of Rep. Derrick ), https://perma.cc/N2AP-
ZVBF. Assault weapons had become “the weapons of
choice among drug dealers, criminal gangs, hate
groups, and mentally deranged persons bent on mass
murder.” H.R. Rep. No. 103- 489, at 13. As a result,
police forces were “required to upgrade their service
weapons merely as a matter of self-defense.” Id. at 13–
14. The weapons’ military fe atures were found to be
“not merely cosmetic,” but instead to “serve specific,
combat-functional ends.” Id. at 18. Unlike the 650
sporting guns the Assault Weapons Ban expressly
exempted, these weapons were “used by criminals, not
hunters or sport shooters,” and their “sole purpose . . .
is to kill a lot of people  quickly.” 140 Cong. Rec. 9338
(May 5, 1994) (statement  of Rep. Derrick),
https://perma.cc/N2AP-ZVBF.
Moreover, subsequent research has corroborated
Congress’s carefully considered judgment, showing
that the 1994 Assault Weap ons Ban coincided with
significant reductions in criminal use of assault
weapons and fewer deadly mass shootings during the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban period (1994–2004). For
example, a 2004 study commissioned by the National
Institute of Justice found that assault weapons fell
from 5.4 percent of ATF crime-gun traces in 1992–
1993 to 1.6 percent in 2001–2002, a decline of 70
percent. William J. Krouse, Cong. Rsch. Serv.,
RL32585, Semiautomatic Assault Weapons Ban  19
(2004). Local police data pointed the same way: in the
six localities studied, assault weapons “typically fell
by one-third or more as a share of firearms used in
crime” from the late 1990s through 2002. Id. at 20.
This research confirms what Congress reasonably

7


believed based on extensive evidence at the time the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban was adopted: assault
weapons are unusually dangerous and pose unique
threats to public safety that undermine law-abiding
citizens’ overall ability to effectively defend
themselves. Assault weapons bans reduce violence by
keeping these unusually lethal instruments off the
streets.
III. The expiration of the 1994 Assault Weapons
Ban in 2004 was a product of constitutionally
appropriate legislative policymaking and did not
reflect a judgment by Congress that the Second
Amendment stood in the way of a continued
nationwide ban on AR-15-style assault weapons. To
the contrary, even Second Amendment absolutists
such as then-Senator (and former Attorney General)
John Ashcroft criticized the policy wisdom of the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban but squarely affirmed that the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban did not violate the
Constitution. Numerous Republican Representatives
and Senators publicly supported an extension of the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban, and then-President
George W. Bush himself indicated that it should have
been extended. Congress clearly had the authority in
2004 to keep these weapons out of our communities
and protect the safety of the public and law
enforcement by renewing and extending the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban while remaining consistent
with the Second Amendment.
This Court should reject Petitioners’ and the
federal government’s misguided “‘use it or lose it’ view
of legislative authority,” United States v. Rahimi, 602
U.S. 680, 740 (2024) (Barrett,  J., concurring)—under

8


which Congress and State Legislatures would
confront a rapidly closing Second Amendment window
that requires them to act quickly or not at all in
response to highly dangerous new weapons
technologies that gain popularity in the commercial
market. Under Petitioners’ theory, if a legislature
does not regulate an unusually dangerous new
weapon before it becomes prevalent, the legislature
somehow forfeits its constitutional authority and
allows the breadth of the Second Amendment right to
rapidly expand and encompass new weaponry in a
matter of a few years. That cannot be right: the ambit
of the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms
is grounded in historical tradition and cannot hinge
loosely upon the short-term popularity of particular
new weapons incorporating rapidly advancing
weapons technologies. In the 22 years since the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban lapsed, AR-15 platform assault
weapons have proliferated, but such weapons have
become no less unusual and extraordinary in their
power to inflict mayhem, increase risks to law
enforcement, and threaten public safety. By the same
token, federal and state legislative authority to
express the People’s will by regulating such weaponry
cannot reasonably be held to have shrunk in its
constitutional scope over such a short span of years.
Amici respectfully submit that this Court should
affirm the judgments of the Seventh and Second
Circuits in these consolidated cases. The Court’s
Heller decision leaves no doubt that the Second
Amendment right is “not a right to keep and carry any
weapon whatsoever in any manner and for whatever
purpose.” 554 U.S. at 626. While the Second
Amendment may take some issues “off the table,” id.

9


at 636, it does not prev ent the People’s elected
representatives from prohibiting assault weapons
found by Congress, State Legislatures, or local
governments to pose unusual dangers to civilians and
law enforcement. Congress reached that judgment on
an extensive record in 1994, and nothing about the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban’s expiration a decade later
or other developments since then can be construed to
deprive the People’s representatives of constitutional
authority to reach the same judgment today.
ARGUMENT
I. As Strong Supporters of the Second
Amendment, Dozens of Republican Elected
Officials Recognized That the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban Stood Well Within the Nation’s
Historical Tradition of Gun Regulation.
The 1994 Assault Weapons Ban was passed with
bipartisan support that included 38 Republican
Representatives, 10 Republican Senators, and former
Republican Presidents—all of whom believed that the
prohibition of the specified weapons was a reasonable
public-safety measure consistent with a strong
respect for the rights protected by the Second
Amendment.
To be sure, elected officials in the lead-up to the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban were not arguing over
launcegayes or Bowie knives. In enacting the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban, however, Congress most
certainly was responding to “unprecedented societal
concerns” caused by “dramatic technological changes,”
N.Y. State. Rifle & Pi stol Ass’n v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1,

10


27 (2022), which had produc ed a new category of
unusually dangerous weapons that were inflicting
wanton violence against the American people. For
example, in 1984, a gunman armed with an Uzi
carbine and other firearms killed 21 people at a
McDonald’s restaurant in San Ysidro, California. See
Michael Granberry, A 77-Minute Moment in History
That Will Never Be Forgotten , L.A. Times (July 16,
1989), https://perma.cc/Z68R-RX8D. In 1989, a
gunman with an AK-47 and a 75-round magazine
fired 106 rounds in less than  two minutes into the
schoolyard of Cleveland Elementary School in
Stockton, California, killing five children and
wounding 29 others. H.R. Rep. No. 103-489, at 15;
Opp’n Br. for Resps. 2, Viramontes v. Cook County, No.
25-238 (U.S. Oct. 29, 2025). In 1993, a gunman with
two TEC-DC9 assault pistols and 50-round magazines
killed eight people at 101 California Street in San
Francisco, and another gunman, reloading 15-round
magazines, killed six commuters on the Long Island
Rail Road. H.R. Rep. No. 103-489, at 14–15.
The 1994 Assault Weapons Ban was not a sudden
swerve away from prior regulations addressing new
weapons technologies, but rather a measured and
proportional action consistent with prior legislative
and executive initiatives. In the 1930s, Congress
responded to the advent of fully automatic weaponry
by passing the National Firearms Act of 1934,
imposing a stringent registration scheme for
automatic weapons as well as prohibitive taxes on
their transfer. See Pub. L. No. 73-474, 48 Stat. 1236

11


(1934).2 AR-15 platform semi-automatic weapons
were not designed until the late 1950s, as a result of a
U.S. military request for a lightweight, high-velocity
rifle comparable in firepower to the Soviet AK-47. See
Dallas T. Durham, The M-16: Tradition, Innovation,
and Controversy, U.S. Army Command & Gen. Staff
Coll. (2021). The potential for mayhem associated
with these weapons materialized over the ensuing
decades. In 1989, the George H.W. Bush
administration responded to growing concerns by
taking executive action to impose a permanent import
ban on 43 types of assault rifles. Charles Mohr, U.S.
Bans Imports of Assault Rifles in Shift by Bush , N.Y.
Times (Mar. 15, 1989), https://perma.cc/432N-MEYW;
Susan F. Rasky, Import Ban on Assault Rifles
Becomes Permanent, N.Y. Times (July 8, 1989),
https://perma.cc/SYH6-L8QJ. Five years later, as
Congress was considering the 1994 Assault Weapons
Ban, former President Ronald Reagan commended
the “impressive 40% drop in imported assault
weapons traced to crime between 1989 and 1991”; but
President Reagan urged Congress to support the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban because the “killing continues.”
162 Cong. Rec. H3763–H3764 (daily ed. June 14,
2016), https://perma.cc/5ULG-XDRJ.
Against this backdrop, support for the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban crossed party lines in Congress.
Amici supported the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban, not
despite their deep commitment to the Second

2 This Court affirmed the constitutionality of the National
Firearms Act in United States v. Miller, 307 U.S. 174, 178 (1939);
see also Heller, 554 U.S. at 627 (acknowledging that M-16 rifles
“may be banned”).

12


Amendment, but consistent with it. Amici understood,
as this Court later held, that the Second Amendment
protects an individual right to bear arms, but that
right is “not unlimited” and does not guarantee “a
right to keep and carry any weapon whatsoever in any
manner whatsoever and for whatever purpose.”
Heller, 554 U.S. at 626. The United States had already
sharply restricted fully automatic machine guns to
military uses and barred the importation of most
foreign semi-automatic weap ons. Mass violence and
horrific injuries and death left no doubt that AR-15-
style assault weapons are highly dangerous and pose
unusual threats. Support for the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban was entirely consistent with the Second
Amendment’s protection of citizens’ right to keep and
bear arms for lawful self-defense.
Floor statements in the House debate on the 1994
standalone bill to ban assault weapons reflect House
Republicans’ abiding commitments to the Second
Amendment right. Amicus Christopher Shays (CT-4)
strongly affirmed that he believed “Americans have
the constitutional right and protection to bear arms,”
but—in the face of the violence and disorder caused by
the proliferation of assault weapons—the
“Government has the constitutional responsibility to
regulate that right.” 140 Cong. Rec. 9372 (May 5,
1994), https://perma.cc/N2AP-ZVBF.  Representative
Sherwood Boehlert (NY-23) similarly pointed out that
Second Amendment rights are fundamental but not
absolute, and he analogized the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban to the reas onable limits that the
Constitution permits on the freedoms of speech and
press. 140 Cong. Rec. 9369 (May 5, 1994).

13


Numerous other Republicans with a deep
commitment to the Second Amendment also
recognized the compelling public safety justification
for the 1994 Assault Weapon s Ban, as well as the
absence of any Second Amendment barrier to its
enactment. For example, Representative Rick Lazio
(NY-2) affirmed that, while he was “a staunch
supporter of the [S]econd [A]mendment,” assault
weapons are highly dangerous and can be regulated
without jeopardizing individuals’ constitutional
rights. 140 Cong. Rec. 9353 (May 5, 1994),
https://perma.cc/J69K-4B7E. Representative Lazio
stated that he did “not believe that these weapons—
whose functions are so adaptable to the destruction of
human life—are protected under [S]econd
[A]mendment rights.” Id. He concluded by stating
that if assault weapons were protected by the Second
Amendment, he would oppose the bill. Id. Similarly,
Representative Bill Young (FL-10), another strong
defender of Americans’ right to own guns, stated that
he could not support allowing the continued
production of the specified assault weapons for use by
anyone other than a member of the Nation’s
uniformed services or law enforcement agencies. 140
Cong. Rec. 9375–76 (May 5, 1994). These statements
reflect the same principle later recognized in Heller
and its progeny: a commitment to the individual right
to keep and bear arms can coexist with reasonable
restrictions on unusually  dangerous weapons to
protect the public.3

3 H.R. 3355 (103rd): Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement
Act of 1994  (Aug. 25, 1994), https://perma.cc/U8SE-GVSA.
(continued…)

14


These Republican members of Congress were far
from alone in their Second Amendment judgment:
they were also forcefully supported by former
Republican Presidents, who joined former President
Jimmy Carter in publicly  advocating for the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban. In a joint letter to Congress
signed by Presidents Gerald Ford, Carter, and
Reagan, the former Presidents described the problem
of assault weapons as “a matter of vital importance to
the public safety” because, among other things, such
weapons already accounted for a disproportionate
share of “guns traced to  crime.” 162 Cong. Rec.
H3763–H3764 (daily ed. June 14, 2016),
https://perma.cc/5ULG-XDRJ. President Reagan went
even further in his efforts to ensure the legislation’s
passage, lobbying individual Republican legislators
and sending additional letters urging legislators to
pass the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban.  Andrew
Kaczynski, The Assault Weapon Ban Would Have
Never Passed If It Wasn’t for Ronald Reagan ,
BuzzFeed News, (Dec. 19, 2012)
https://perma.cc/4DZF-7RYP.
Ten years later, when the 1994 Assault Weapons
Ban was up for renewal, th en-President George W.
Bush—a “longstanding advocate of the rights of gun
owners in America” 4—added his voice in support of
the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban and backed its

Representative Young supported the standalone 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban but voted against the omnibus bill.
4 Statement on the United States Supreme Court Ruling on
Individual Gun Rights, Am. Presidency Project (June 26, 2008),
https://perma.cc/8FXN-JW2A.

15


reauthorization. Washington in Brief , Wash. Post
(Apr. 11, 2003), https://pe rma.cc/FK7C-GG2P. Even
after the 1994 Assault Weap ons Ban lapsed in 2004,
President Bush maintained that he favored extending
it, stating in a 2004 debate that he believed Congress
“ought to extend the [A]ssault [W]eapons [B]an.”
Transcript: Bush, Kerry Debate Domestic Policies ,
CNN (Oct. 14, 2004), https: //perma.cc/A49F-BL8J.
President Bush recognized, as did many Republican
leaders before him, that commitment to protecting
Second Amendment rights and support for the
prohibition of semi-automatic assault weapons were
not at odds but in harmony.
The 1994 Assault Weapons Ban was ultimately
enacted by Congress as part of the Violent Crime
Control and Law Enforcement Act. A total of 38 House
Republicans, including Amici, voted for the
standalone assault-weapons legislation, and ten
Republican Senators supported the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban, introduced as the Feinstein
Amendment to the 1993 Senate omnibus crime bill. 5

President Bill Clinton signed the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban into law on September 13, 1994.
The 1994 Assault Weapons Ban prohibited the
manufacture, transfer, or possession of specified
assault weapons, targeting 19 specified firearms (and
their copies), while also establishing a features-based
test for semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns
possessing two or more enumerated military-style
features. It separately prohibited large-capacity
ammunition feeding devices holding more than ten
rounds. Congress also expressly exempted from the
prohibition more than 650 firearms commonly used
for hunting and sport; grandfathered weapons and
magazines already lawfully possessed; required a
study by the Department of Justice of the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban’s effectiveness; and included a
sunset provision whereby the law would lapse after
ten years, in 2004, unless reauthorized by Congress.
The 1994 Assault Weapons Ban is substantially
similar to the Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois
statutes that are challenged here. Connecticut and
Cook County employ the same basic regulatory
architecture as the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban: each
provides a features-based definition, identifies
specific assault weapons, including specified models
and their copies, and separately restricts magazines

II. Congress Correctly Found That Assault
Weapons Were Unusually Dangerous—a
Judgment Confirmed by the Sharp Drop in
Gun Violence During the Ban Period.
In enacting the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban,
Congress did not act precipitately or on the basis of
emotion or whim. To the contrary, over five years of
congressional hearings, the House and Senate
developed an extensive record demonstrating the
disproportionate dangers posed by assault weapons,
including AR-15-style rifles. Relying on this extensive
factual record, Congress found that such weapons
were unusually dangerous. These findings were
confirmed by the significant reductions in gun
violence that prevailed thereafter during the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban period from 1994 to 2004.
The legislative record supporting Congress’s
enactment of the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban
documented the distinctive and unusual dangers
posed by the covered weapons, including the
disproportionate use of assault weapons in crime,
against police, and in mass killings. The then-Director
of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms
testified that assault weapons were
disproportionately more often used in crimes. H.R.
Rep. No. 103-489, at 13. Th e record showed that
assault weapons dramatically increased the firepower
available to perpetrators of violent crime. Id. at 14.
The House Judiciary Comm ittee likewise found
mounting evidence that assault weapons had become
“the weapons of choice amon g drug dealers, criminal
gangs, hate groups, and mentally deranged persons
bent on mass murder.” Id. In 1993 alone, ATF traced

19


5,397 assault weapons, ro ughly 10 percent of the
55,665 crime guns it traced, with the Colt AR-15
among the most common. 140 Cong. Rec. 3018–19
(Feb. 24, 1994) (statement  of Sen. Feinstein),
https://perma.cc/23YD-YQTY. Law-enforcement
testimony reinforced that concern: officers reported
that “it is not at all unusual for a cop to look down the
barrel of a TEC-9 with a 32 round clip,” and the
Committee found that police departments were being
forced “to upgrade their service weapons merely as a
matter of self-defense.” Id. at 13–14.
The record also identified characteristics of assault
weapons that magnified those dangers. The House
Judiciary Committee explained that most covered
weapons were equipped with 30-round magazines,
allowing “a single person with a single assault weapon
[to] easily fire literally  hundreds of rounds within
minutes,” in contrast to hunting rifles and shotguns
that typically held only three to five rounds. Id. at 18–
19. Those findings drew support from legislators
across the political spectrum. Republican
Representative and Judiciary Committee member
Henry Hyde reversed his previous opposition and
supported the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban, explaining:
“I believe in the right to own weapons, protect your
home or property or hunt. . . . But these are dangerous
weapons.” Karen Hosler, Assault Gun Ban Faces

https://perma.cc/4DUD-RS53 (emphasis added).
House Republican leader Robert Michel similarly
explained that, “[w]hen our police need to increase
their firepower so that they can match the firepower
of the criminals, it is time to ban assault weapons .”
See Kenneth J. Cooper, House Backs Ban on Assault

20


Guns, Wash. Post (May 5, 1994),
https://perma.cc/JB9U-7A3K. Congress thus acted on
extensive evidence that assault weapons presented
unusual dangers to the public and law enforcement,
including their disproportionate use in crime and
capacity for sustained fire.
Witnesses to several of these attacks also testified
before the Judiciary Committee. The Judiciary
Committee's report recounts that, just months before
the House acted in 1994, Los Angeles police officer
Christy Hamilton was killed with an AR-15. H.R. Rep.
No. 103-489, at 14–15. The House then debated the
standalone bill for five hours before passing it 216 to
214, with 38 Republicans voting in favor. See 140
Cong. Rec. H3063 (daily ed. May 5, 1994). Congress
enacted the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban on the basis
of that extensive evidentiary record.
The evidence persuaded Amici and their fellow
legislators that the military features of these weapons
were not cosmetic, but combat-functional, producing
“a capability for lethality—more wounds, more
serious, in more victims—far beyond that of other
firearms in general, including other semiautomatic
guns.” N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n, Inc. v. Cuomo ,
804 F.3d 242, 262 (2d Cir. 2015). Under the 1994 law,
Amici and their fellow members of Congress did not
seek to suppress overall gun ownership or hamper
Americans’ ability to defend themselves effectively.
Congress instead sought to reduce the harms
associated with the use of a well-defined category of
unusually dangerous weapons and magazines
identified in the legislative record.

Moreover, the follow-up studies that Congress

was achieving that objective. A Justice Departmentfunded study found that, in the 1994 Assault Weapons
Ban’s very first year, traces of assault weapons

Subsequent research has provided further
evidence that the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban
coincided with fewer and less deadly mass shootings.
A 2019 peer-reviewed stud y found that, after

Associated with the 1994–2004 Federal Assault

the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban “resulted in a
significant decrease in public mass shootings, number

More recently, a 2024 study examining public

The public-safety impact of the 1994 Assault

unusually dangerous and attr active to criminals and

comprised only about one percent of all guns in

III. The Scope of the Second Amendment Should
Not Vary Depending on Historically
Contingent Short-Term Changes in the
Popularity of Highly Dangerous Weapons.
There is no doubt that AR-15 platform semiautomatic assault weapons are much more widely
owned by American citizens today than they were in
1994. Since such ownership exploded after the 1994
Assault Weapons Ban lapsed in 2004, that current
state of affairs might not exist if Congress had
extended the ban, as then-President George W. Bush
and numerous other Second Amendment supporters
recommended. But regardless of any such
hypothetical consequences, this Court has repeatedly
recognized that Congress does not always legislate to
the constitutional ceiling, and the scope of individual
rights under the Constitution does not wax or wane
like the moon. The mere fact that weapons ownership
increased after Congress allowed the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban to lapse—or that more State
legislatures have not joined the eleven States that ban
or sharply restrict AR-15-style assault weapons—
cannot be construed as a basis for concluding that the
Constitution now forbids such restrictions.
Indeed, as Justice Barrett has observed in the
Second Amendment context, it is a “serious problem[]”
to “assume[] that founding-era legislatures maximally
exercised their power to regulate, thereby adopting a
‘use it or lose it’ view of legislative authority.” United
States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680, 739–40 (2024)
(Barrett, J., concurring). The 2004 failure of Congress
to extend the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban concisely
reinforces the same point in a more recent timeframe.

25


The extension faltered because the Senate rejected
the gun-industry liability bill to which the
reauthorization amendment had been attached. The
Assault Weapons Ban: Lessons about Congress , Gov’t
Affs. Inst. (Jan. 16, 2013), https://perma.cc/SM9P-
58RS. But then-President Bush supported the
reauthorization, a bipartisan Senate majority voted
52-47 to extend the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban, and
polls showed that roughly two-thirds of Americans
favored renewal. Republican Representative Michael
Castle (R-Del.) put it plainly: “To allow the ban to
sunset is simply irresponsible; every major law
enforcement organization in America supports an
extension of the ban.” 162 Cong. Rec. H3763–H3764
(daily ed. June 14, 2016), https://perma.cc/5ULG-
XDRJ. In 2004, there was no serious question that
Congress had the legislative authority under the
Constitution to continue the 1994 Assault Weapons
Ban indefinitely. While Congress failed to exercise its
full power to regulate in 2004, that failure to regulate
maximally does not forfeit th at authority or give it a
short-term shelf life of only a handful of years.
Congress’s failure to reauthorize the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban in 2004 did not reflect, and should not
be construed as reflecting , any concerns about the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban’s validity under the
Second Amendment. See Br. of Ronnell Higgins, in his
Official Capacity as Commissioner of Connecticut
Dept. of Emergency Services and Public Protection, et
al, at 49–50. To the contrary, as noted above, then-
President George W. Bush supported extension of the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban and lamented the fact
that it did not pass in 2004. If anything, AR-15
platform assault weapons were less prevalent in 2004

26


than they had been in 1994, when the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban was imposed.
Nor can constitutional significance be assigned to
Congress’s timing given that state and local
legislatures exercised their regulatory authority on
roughly equivalent schedules. Congress did not
legislate in a vacuum. As it debated the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban, state and local governments were
independently addressing the same issue.
Connecticut enacted its assault weapons ban on June
29, 1993, and Cook County followed that autumn,
adopting its ordinance on October 19 and amending it
on November 16, 1993, one day before the Senate
adopted Senator Feinstein’s amendment. These laws
were also part of the broader wave of state legislation
following the 1989 Stockton schoolyard shooting,
including measures enacted in California in 1989,
New Jersey in 1990, and Maryland in 1994. When the
federal ban later expired, state and local regulation
did not disappear with it: Cook County reenacted its
ordinance as the Blair Holt Assault Weapons Ban in
2006 and revised it in 2013, while Connecticut
updated its law in 2013 and again in 2023. That
history underscores the error in treating a particular
legislature’s decision to act or not act as a marker of
the constitutional boundary for all legislatures
thereafter.
The distinction between legislative policy choices
and constitutional limits is evident in the views of the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban’s opponents. Even some of
the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban’s most prominent
Republican critics drew a line between policy and
constitutionality. Senator John Ashcroft, a staunch

27


supporter of the Second Amendment, who
“unequivocally” believed the Constitution protects the
right of individuals to own guns, is a clear example.
Dan Eggen, Ashcroft: Gun Ownership an Individual
Right; Letter to NRA Sparks Debate Over 2nd
Amendment, Long Interpreted as Applying
Collectively, Wash. Post (May 23, 2001),
https://perma.cc/7LMM-FBHB. Then-Attorney
General-designate Ashcroft publicly criticized the
1994 Assault Weapons Ban, calling it “wrongheaded.” Attorney General Nominee John Ashcroft’s
Senate Confirmation Hearing (Day Two) , Am.
Presidency Project (Jan. 17, 2001),
https://perma.cc/B55C-T48F. However, when asked
under oath whether the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban
violated the Second Amendment, Ashcroft answered
without qualification: “No.” He then clarified that he
did not “believe the Second Amendment to be one that
forbids any regulation of guns.” Id. Senator Ashcroft
distinguished his policy opposition to the 1994 Assault
Weapons Ban from its consti tutionality: “[T]here are
a number of enactments which I would not prefer as
policy, but which I believe would be
constitutional. . . . I believe that there are
constitutional inhibitions on the rights of citizens to
bear certain kinds of arms. And some of those I would
think good judgment, some of those I’d think bad
judgment.” Id. Senator Ashcroft’s testimony
illustrates the distinction between constitutional
judgment and policy preference.
Under Petitioners’ theory, legislative restraint
would have the anomalous effect of narrowing the
government’s regulatory authority as weapons that
are unusual in their lethality and capacity for

28


intimidation and terror become more commonly
“used.” That cannot be right. A legislature does not
forfeit constitutional authority by deciding—for
whatever short-term combination of political reasons,
or no demonstrable reason at all—not to exercise it at
any given time. An increase in the popularity of
assault weapons during a temporal gap in regulation
cannot rewrite the boundaries of the Constitution.
The Second Amendment’s scope depends on
constitutional text and history, not whether
legislatures exercise their lawful authority at any
particular moment.
